hints: Look closely at the words xylem vessel elements. Think about their shape: very narrow, hollow tubes with walls that water can stick to.
Recall why water molecules stick to each other and to walls. What type of bond between water molecules makes cohesion, adhesion and movement up narrow tubes possible?
walkthrough:
**Start with the xylem vessel**

Think of xylem vessels as very narrow, continuous straws from roots to leaves. Water has to move up them, often against gravity.

In narrow tubes, water can rise a little by itself. This is capillary action.

**Remember why water is so sticky**

Water is a polar molecule, so hydrogen bonds form between water molecules. This gives two vital properties.

Cohesion is water sticking to water. Adhesion is water sticking to the xylem wall (2). Both depend on hydrogen bonding (3).

**Put 1, 2 and 3 together**

Hydrogen bonding holds the water column together so transpiration pull from above does not break it. Adhesion helps the column grip the walls and resist gravity. Capillary action in the narrow vessels also helps lift water.

So all three features, 1, 2 and 3, play a role.

options.A: Correct. Capillary action, adhesion to walls, and hydrogen bonding (which causes cohesion) all help support the continuous column of water in xylem.
options.B: Incomplete. It correctly includes 1 and 2 but wrongly leaves out hydrogen bonding, which is the basis for cohesion and adhesion.
options.C: Incomplete. It correctly includes 1 and 3 but wrongly leaves out adhesion, which helps water stick to xylem walls and move up.
options.D: Incomplete. It correctly includes 2 and 3 but wrongly leaves out capillary action, which assists water rise in narrow xylem vessels.
